entries.topic: Unit 101, the Qibya raid (14–15 October 1953), Israel's denial, and Security Council Resolution 101

sources.label: "General Ariel (Arik) Sharon", IDF and Defense Establishment Archives, Israel Ministry of Defense
"The 1953 Qibya Raid Revisited: Excerpts from Moshe Sharett's Diaries", introduced by Walid Khalidi, annotated by Neil Caplan, Journal of Palestine Studies 31:4 (Summer 2002), pp. 77–98
"Israeli Attack on Qibya (October 1953)", Jewish Virtual Library
"Ben-Gurion Blames Qibya Provocation on Arab States' War Policy", Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 21 October 1953
Department of State Press Release No. 572, 18 October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 695)
"The Qibya (Israel-Jordan) Incident: United Nations Security Council Resolution, November 24, 1953", Avalon Project, Yale Law School
Security Council Resolution 101 (1953) of 24 November 1953, UNISPAL
UN Security Council, 632nd meeting (S/PV.632), 29 October 1953, UNISPAL

claims.text: According to the Israel Ministry of Defense archives, Ariel Sharon was appointed in August 1953 to establish and command Unit 101, created "to carry out reprisal operations in enemy territory"; in January 1954 the unit was folded into paratrooper battalion 890 under his command, and he later commanded Paratroopers Brigade 202, under which cross-border operations continued.

Khalidi and Caplan describe Sharon in 1953 as a 25-year-old major who conceived and planned the Qibya raid and commanded Unit 101; they also record that he led an attack on the al-Burj refugee camp in Gaza in late August 1953 in which, per Benny Morris, twenty people were killed (including seven women and five children) and twenty-two wounded.

The raid followed an attack at Yehud (spelled Tiryat Yehuda by the Jewish Virtual Library) on the night of 12–13 October 1953 in which a grenade thrown into a house killed Suzanne Kinyas and her two children; the Jordanian-Israeli Mixed Armistice Commission called that attack "intolerable aggression", as Israel's representative Eban reminded the Security Council.

Per Khalidi and Caplan, the planning options included "total destruction of the village and maximum harm to the villagers"; Dayan authorized Sharon to choose, and the decision was to retaliate "in the firmest possible manner". The Jewish Virtual Library quotes Sharon's diary: "Qibya was to be an example for everyone."

Khalidi and Caplan give forty-five houses blown up and sixty-nine villagers killed, all civilians, about three-quarters of them women and children; Glubb's count was sixty-six. The Jewish Virtual Library gives 50 homes and 69 civilians.
Sharon later wrote in his autobiography Warrior that he had not known the houses were occupied ("I couldn't believe my ears"), suggesting families had stayed inside expecting only limited damage.

In a radio broadcast on the evening of 19 October 1953, Ben-Gurion denied "the absurd and fantastic allegation that 600 men of the Israel defense forces took part", said "not a single Army unit was absent from its base" that night, attributed the raid to border settlers whose patience had been exhausted by the Yehud killings, and said "all the responsibility rests with the government of Transjordan" while regretting that innocent people were killed.

Sharett's diary shows the cover story was a deliberate choice: Ben-Gurion insisted the army not admit responsibility and that border residents "had taken the law into their own hands"; Sharett noted it would not be believed, and Ben-Gurion called the UN observer's contrary account a "fantastic lie" in a marginal note.
Sharett wrote on 16 October 1953 that had he feared "such a slaughter" he "would have raised hell", and that "Horror gripped me" on hearing Jordanian radio describe the destruction.

On 18 October 1953 the State Department expressed "the deepest sympathy for the families of those who lost their lives in and near Qibya", described an attack "by Israeli forces", said those responsible "should be brought to account", and joined Britain and France in asking the Security Council to consider the frontier with a direct report from General Vagn Bennike.

Resolution 101 of 24 November 1953 found that the "retaliatory action at Qibya by Israeli armed forces" violated the cease-fire and was inconsistent with the Armistice Agreement and the Charter, expressed "the strongest censure", and called on Israel to prevent such actions; it also noted "substantial evidence" of unauthorized crossings of the demarcation line and asked Jordan to strengthen its measures against them.

Resolution 101 was adopted at the 642nd meeting by 9 votes to none, with Lebanon and the Soviet Union abstaining, and asked the Chief of Staff to report within three months, taking account of Israel's request for a conference under Article XII of the Armistice Agreement.

disputes.question: How many houses were destroyed and how many people were killed at Qibya?

positions.view: Forty-five houses; sixty-nine villagers killed, all civilians (Khalidi and Caplan; also Volume II's figure).
Fifty homes; 69 civilians (Jewish Virtual Library); Glubb counted sixty-six dead.
Israel's official line at the time: no army unit left its base; enraged border settlers acted (Ben-Gurion, 19 October 1953).
Israeli regular forces under Sharon (Resolution 101; the State Department; Sharett's diary recording that the settler story was a chosen cover; Sharon's own later account).

entries.topic: The Banat Yaacov works in the Syrian demilitarized zone and the US suspension of aid (September–October 1953)

sources.label: Memorandum of conversation, Dulles–Eban–Shiloah, c. 25 September 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 673)
Secretary of State's press and radio news conference, 20 October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 698)
Secretary of State's news conference, 27 October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 709)
Department of State Press Release No. 604, "Aid to Israel", statement by Secretary Dulles, October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 711)
Security Council Resolution 100 (1953), 27 October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 710)

claims.text: Israel began the works in the Israel–Syria demilitarized zone at Banat Yaacov on 2 September 1953; Eban told Dulles it was "an electric power project" begun with the knowledge of UNTSO's Colonel Tillotson and that no water would actually be diverted until sometime in 1954.

On 23 September 1953 General Bennike, UNTSO Chief of Staff, asked Israel to "cease its operations in the demilitarized zone" pending agreement; Sharett replied with reservations on 24 September and Syria complained to the UN on 12 October.

In that conversation (about 25 September 1953) Dulles said he would "withhold release of MSA funds until the issue of the Jordan waters had been further clarified", on Assistant Secretary Byroade's advice; Eban asked him to keep US aid and the water dispute separate.

At his 20 October 1953 press conference Dulles said no allocation had yet gone to Israel because "as long as the State of Israel was acting in defiance of that decision" it was questionable whether to make it, and that the deferral followed Bennike's decision, not "the more recent incidents"; he put the total sum "in the neighborhood of $100,000,000" after an aide suggested $50–60 million.

On 27 October 1953 Dulles added that no new economic-assistance allocations had been made from the fiscal-year fund "either to Israel or any Arab state", and declined to discuss the deferment while the Security Council was seized of it.

Resolution 100, adopted unanimously on 27 October 1953 at the 631st meeting on a French draft, deemed it desirable that the works begun on 2 September be suspended during the Council's examination, noted Eban's undertaking to suspend them "without prejudice" to the merits, and relied on the Chief of Staff to confirm compliance; Bennike later reported the works stopped at midnight on 28 October.

In Press Release No. 604, issued the day after the resolution, Dulles said "the impediment to the present grant of economic aid to Israel has been removed" and recommended about $26 million for the first six months of the fiscal year, the amount tentatively earmarked under the Mutual Security Act of 1953; granting aid while Israel ignored the UN request, he said, "would tend to undermine the authority" of UNTSO.
The Security Council's consideration of the Banat Yaacov question ran from its 629th to its 656th meeting, 27 October 1953 to 22 January 1954.

disputes.question: How much US aid was at stake in the 1953 suspension?

positions.view: About $26 million for the first half of the fiscal year (Press Release 604).

Dulles at his 20 October press conference recalled a total 'in the neighborhood of $100,000,000' (his aide had said $50–60 million); these figures refer to the year's programme, not the released tranche.

entries.topic: The Johnston mission and the Jordan Valley Unified Plan (October 1953–October 1955)

sources.label: Statement by the President on Eric Johnston's Mission to the Near East, 16 October 1953, American Presidency Project
Telegram from the Acting Secretary of State to the Embassy in the United Kingdom, October 1953 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 1, doc. 685)
Circular airgram from the Department of State to certain posts on the Jordan waters (FRUS 1961–1963, vol. XVIII, doc. 355)

"Integrated Management and Negotiations for Equitable Allocation of Flow of the Jordan River Among Riparian States", AquaPedia case study (analysis by Aaron T. Wolf, Joshua T. Newton and Matthew Pritchard)
"The Johnston Mission: Background & Overview", Jewish Virtual Library

claims.text: On 16 October 1953 Eisenhower sent Eric Johnston "as my personal representative with the rank of Ambassador" to discuss "the mutual development of the water resources of the Jordan River Valley on a regional basis", noting that "some hundreds of thousands of Arab refugees" lacked adequate support and that a valley plan could give "a substantial proportion" of them an economic base on the land.

A State Department telegram of October 1953 explained the urgency: a TVA engineering study made for UNRWA had "just been completed", its findings "cannot be carried out without political agreement on the part of the riparian states", the best refugee settlement lay in the East and West Ghor, and "Israel's unilateral action in commencing diversion of water in the Demilitarized Zone below Lake Huleh" had raised tension.
The same telegram noted that the plan would require Israel to relinquish "exclusive territorial control over the outlets to Lake Tiberias".

The Main plan, drawn up by Charles T. Main for the TVA on UNRWA's commission, explicitly did not "consider political factors or attempt to set this system into the national boundaries now prevailing"; Israel answered with the Cotton plan, which brought in the Litani, and the Arab League Technical Committee, under Egyptian leadership, produced an Arab plan in 1954 that excluded the Litani and rejected storage in the Sea of Galilee.

AquaPedia tabulates the competing allocations (million cubic metres a year): Main — Israel 394, Jordan 774, Syria 45; Cotton — Israel 1,290 (including 400 from the Litani), Jordan 575, Lebanon 450, Syria 30; Arab plan — Israel 182, Jordan 698, Lebanon 35, Syria 132; Unified (Johnston) plan — Israel 400, Jordan 720, Lebanon 35, Syria 132.

The State Department's later summary gives the Unified Plan's fixed allocations as Jordan 720 mcm (377 from the Yarmuk, 100 from the Jordan, 243 from side wadis), Syria 132 (20 Banias, 22 Jordan, 90 Yarmuk), Lebanon 35 (Hasbani) and Israel 25 from the Yarmuk, with the remaining Jordan waters available to Israel; AquaPedia notes Israel's residue was estimated at about 409 mcm on average.

Johnston signed memoranda of understanding with Israel on 5 July 1955 and with the Arab riparian states' Technical Committee on 11 October 1955, and was told the plan was technically acceptable to Israel, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon; the United States offered to fund two-thirds of development costs.

The Arab League's political organs did not endorse the plan; the State Department records that the Political Committee returned it to the Technical Committee for "further consideration", and AquaPedia dates the League Council's decision not to accept it to October 1955, citing "the political implications of accepting".

AquaPedia's analysts give the Arab reasons as reluctance to imply recognition of Israel through a final agreement, suspicion that the plan favoured Israel, and fear that Negev irrigation would enable more immigration and expansion, with Iraq and Saudi Arabia urging Lebanon, Syria and Jordan not to accept; Nasser, they note, had been an active advocate.

Although never ratified, the allocations were generally adhered to and the United States tied later water-project funding to them; the Jewish Virtual Library says about 200,000 refugees could have been settled on irrigated land in Jordan and that the mission was abandoned in late 1955.

disputes.question: Why did the Unified Plan fail?

positions.view: Political: accepting a shared water regime implied recognition of Israel; Arab governments under pressure from Iraq and Saudi Arabia declined it (AquaPedia analysis; State Department summary).
Substantive Arab objections: the plan was seen as designed to Israel's benefit and as enabling immigration and expansion in the Negev (Arab positions as summarized by the same analysts).

entries.topic: Ben-Gurion's withdrawal and return, Sharett's premiership, and the 'activist' versus 'moderate' split (1953–1956), with the diaries and their uses

sources.label: "The security portfolio was imposed on me…", David Ben-Gurion and the IDF exhibition, IDF and Defense Establishment Archives (quoting Ben-Gurion to the Knesset, 31 October 1965)
"Past Governments", Prime Minister's Office, State of Israel
"Ben-Gurion Returns to Government", Center for Israel Education
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", International Journal of Middle East Studies 36:4 (November 2004), pp. 657–673
Neil Caplan (intro. and annot.), "The Sinai Campaign Viewed From Asia: Selections From Moshe Sharett's Diaries", Moshe Sharett Heritage Society

"Israeli State Terrorism: An Analysis of the Sharett Diaries", excerpted from Livia Rokach, Israel's Sacred Terrorism (Association of Arab-American University Graduates, 1980), Institute for Palestine Studies
Ben-Gurion to Moshe Sharett, 28 July 1956, letter on Sharett's resignation as foreign minister (dealer's catalogue description and transcription), Seth Kaller Inc.

claims.text: Ben-Gurion told the Knesset in 1965 that the government granted him a long leave on 7 July 1953; on 18 October 1953 he submitted a three-year security plan, which the government ratified; he resigned with the government on 7 December 1953 and retired to Sde Boker on 13 December.

The Prime Minister's Office lists the Fifth Government, under Moshe Sharett, as serving from 26 January 1954 to 29 June 1955, and the Seventh Government, under Ben-Gurion, from 3 November 1955; its listing of the Sixth (Sharett) gives an end date of 3 November 1955 and an apparently garbled start date.
Ben-Gurion said he "returned to the Ministry of Defense with the Knesset approval on February 21, 1955", replacing Pinhas Lavon in Sharett's cabinet after a 14-month semiretirement.

Shlaim describes two schools: Sharett led the "negotiation" school and Ben-Gurion the "retaliation" school; Sharett "sought to avoid escalation in order to prevent war", while Dayan "needed escalation to bring about war".

Caplan writes that Sharett was "deeply troubled by the growing popularity of the competing 'activist' strategy of stiff reprisals" advocated by Ben-Gurion, Dayan and others, led cabinet majorities for restraint, and blocked proposals to capture Gaza or the Straits of Tiran.

Sharett's diary, as translated in Rokach's 1980 study, records Dayan on 31 January 1954 answering "of course" when asked whether his course meant war with Egypt; on 25 January 1955 Lavon proposing to occupy the Gaza Strip and the Syrian demilitarized zone; and Dayan on 26 May 1955 calling retaliation actions "our vital lymph".
Sharett wrote on 1 March 1955, after the Gaza raid: "It is the same old story: hit and run and try to fool the world" (Rokach's translation).

Shlaim records that Dulles offered a mutual defence pact in February 1955 on condition that Israel not expand its borders by force or carry out military retaliation; Ben-Gurion and Sharett accepted the first condition but not the second.

Sharett resigned as foreign minister on 18 June 1956 and Golda Meir succeeded him; in a letter of 28 July 1956 Ben-Gurion wrote that Sharett's continuing at the Foreign Ministry "was not for the good of the country" and that foreign policy must serve security needs.

Shlaim's judgment, quoted by Caplan: "Ben-Gurion failed to topple Nasser but he succeeded in toppling Sharett." Shlaim also writes that Ben-Gurion authorized secret talks in France and forced Sharett's resignation about a week later, "clearing the way for war".
Sharett's diary was first published in self-censored form; his son Yaakov Sharett later incorporated the remaining entries into the multi-volume Yoman Ishi (Personal Diary).

Interpretation (Rokach, 1980): the diaries document a deliberate strategy of provocation, retaliation, expansion and subversion driven by Ben-Gurion's 'activists', with Sharett as a largely powerless moderate. The study was published by an Arab-American academic association with a preface by Michael Adams; it is an argued reading of selected entries, not a neutral edition.

disputes.question: What do Sharett's diaries show about Israeli policy in 1953–1956?

positions.view: A deliberate strategy of provocation and escalation by the activists, toward war and expansion (Rokach, 1980, from translated excerpts).
A real internal contest over policy: Sharett's restraint often prevailed in cabinet and the activist course won only as US arms were refused and France offered them (Caplan; Shlaim).

entries.topic: Operation Susannah (July 1954), the Cairo trial, and the first round of 'the Affair' (1954–1955)

sources.label: "The 'Unfortunate' or the Lavon affair", IDF and Defense Establishment Archives, Israel Ministry of Defense
"Israel honors 9 Egyptian spies", Ynetnews, 30 March 2005
"On this day, Suzannah bombers hanged", Point of No Return (Jewish refugees from Arab countries blog), January 2016
"The Lavon Affair, Mossad's First Operation in Egypt", Raseef22
"Ben-Gurion Returns to Government", Center for Israel Education
Livia Rokach, Israel's Sacred Terrorism (1980), excerpts of Sharett's diary, Institute for Palestine Studies

claims.text: Israel's Defense Ministry archive describes Operation Susannah, in summer 1954, as "a failed Israeli covert operation" in which military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews; Major Motke Ben-Zur commanded Unit 131.

The archive says the bombings were meant to sabotage Egypt's relations with the West while Egypt negotiated with Britain over evacuating the Suez Canal area, and to be blamed on the Muslim Brotherhood, Egyptian Communists or "local nationalists"; targets were Egyptian, American and British-owned cinemas, libraries and American educational centres, with bombs timed to go off hours after closing.

According to Raseef22's reconstruction from Egyptian sources, coded signals went out on Israeli radio on 16 June 1954; devices were placed in Alexandria mailboxes on 2 July; on 14 July the American libraries in Cairo and Alexandria were set alight; and on 23 July devices were planned for a Cairo station, the Rivoli theatre and Alexandria's Metro and Rio cinemas.

On the evening of 23 July 1954 an Alexandria police officer put out Philip Natanson's burning trousers outside the Rio cinema; his arrest led to the others (Raseef22). Point of No Return describes a phosphorus device igniting in his pocket.

Eleven Egyptian Jews were arrested; the trial ran from 11 December 1954 to 27 January 1955. Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar were sentenced to hang, six received long prison terms (Victor Levi, Philip Natanson, Robert Dassa, Marcel Ninio, Meir Meyuhas, Meir Za'afran) and two were acquitted.

Marzouk and Azar were executed in Cairo on 31 January 1955 after Nasser rejected appeals for mercy; two of the arrested died in custody, among them Max Bennett (Meir Max Bineth), whom Raseef22 says took his own life in detention before the trial session.
Avri Elad, the cell's handler, is identified as a double agent; he was later tried in secret in Israel and jailed for ten years (Ynet; Point of No Return).

Who gave the order was disputed from the start: Defence Minister Lavon denied any knowledge, intelligence chief Colonel Binyamin Gibli said he had received a verbal instruction from Lavon, and Chief of Staff Dayan blamed the minister; the archive says Prime Minister Sharett "was kept out of the loop" and that a two-man commission appointed by the prime minister "did not expose the truth".
Lavon resigned in February 1955; Gibli and Ben-Zur were dismissed; Ben-Gurion replaced Lavon as defence minister on 21 February 1955.

Sharett wrote on 14 January 1955 that he "would never have imagined that we could reach such a horrible state of poisoned relations", and elsewhere that even if Lavon "did not give the order, his role in preparing the ground for the Affair is undeniable" (Rokach's translation).
Ynet reports that the attacks caused no casualties; Raseef22's Egyptian-sourced account says people died in the 2 July Alexandria fire. The two accounts conflict.

Israel long denied involvement, including after the 1979 peace treaty; on 30 March 2005 President Moshe Katsav presented certificates to the nine recruited agents (three survivors attended), the first official recognition. Former Mossad deputy chief David Kimche said: "We knew never to go down that road again."
Raseef22 writes that the affair accelerated the founding of Egypt's General Intelligence Directorate in 1955 under Zakaria Mohieddin.

positions.view: Lavon gave a verbal instruction (Gibli's claim; Dayan blamed the minister).
Lavon did not know (Lavon's denial); the 1955 inquiry did not establish the truth; Sharett judged him responsible for 'preparing the ground' even if he gave no order.

disputes.question: Did the July 1954 attacks kill anyone?

positions.view: No casualties (Ynet, 2005).
People died in the 2 July Alexandria fire (Raseef22, from Egyptian sources).

entries.topic: Egypt's revolution: the Free Officers (July 1952), Nasser's rise over Naguib, the Suez base agreement (1954), the Brotherhood, and the 1956 presidency

sources.label: Byron Cannon, "King Farouk of Egypt Is Overthrown", EBSCO Research Starters (2021)
"Nasser elected president", HISTORY.com, This Day in History, 23 June
Editorial note on the Anglo-Egyptian agreement on the Suez Canal base, 1954 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 2, doc. 1348)
"Egypt Once Again Bans the Muslim Brotherhood, Sixty Years Later", Origins: Current Events in Historical Perspective, Ohio State University and Miami University (October 2014)
Telegram from Ambassador Caffery (Cairo) to the Department of State, November 1954 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. IX, part 2, doc. 1370)
Memorandum of conversation between Soviet Ambassador D. S. Solod and Prime Minister G. Nasser, 15 June 1954 (AVPRF; trans. Guy Laron), Wilson Center Digital Archive

claims.text: The Free Officers carried out their coup in Cairo on 23 July 1952, with Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser as leader and Major General Muhammad Naguib as figurehead; King Farouk was dethroned and ordered to leave the country.
HISTORY.com gives the number who took part with Nasser as 89 other Free Officers.

The new regime decreed agricultural land reform in the months after the coup, and the monarchy gave way to a republic in the summer of 1953; Naguib served as prime minister (1952–1954) and president (1953–1954).
In early 1954 a power struggle split the ruling council; by April 1954 Nasser had majority support and the 'April Decrees' removed Naguib from effective power, with Nasser becoming prime minister.

The Anglo-Egyptian Heads of Agreement were initialled on 27 July 1954 and the final agreement signed on 19 October 1954, abrogating the 1936 treaty: British troops would leave the Canal Zone, 1,200 civilian technicians (up to 800 from outside Egypt) would maintain the base, and Britain could return only on an attack on Egypt, any other Arab state or Turkey — Iran and Israel excluded — for a term of seven years.

In the agreement Egypt pledged to uphold "the principles of the 1888 Convention of Constantinople concerning the free use of the Suez Canal", and the accord recognized the Canal as "an integral part of Egypt".

On 26 October 1954 Mahmoud Abdel-Latif, a young member of the Muslim Brotherhood, fired at Nasser in Manshiya Square, Alexandria, as he spoke about the new treaty; Nasser kept speaking. The Origins essay says it is not clear who ordered the attempt.
The Brotherhood was then banned, more than 1,000 members were arrested and a small number executed, and the movement went underground.

The Revolutionary Command Council removed Naguib "from all his functions" in mid-November 1954 (the announcement was planned for 15 November), accusing him of "conniving with Muslim Brotherhood extremists"; Ambassador Caffery noted that Naguib had opposed the Suez agreement.

On 15 June 1954 Nasser told the Soviet ambassador that Britain had stopped arms shipments and blocked supplies from other European states, that Egypt could not meet "a hundredth of its army's needs", and formally asked the Soviet position on selling arms to Egypt.
On 23 June 1956 Nasser, the only candidate, was elected Egypt's first president with 99.95% in a referendum that also approved a new constitution by 99.8%.

entries.topic: The Gaza raid of 28 February 1955 (Operation Black Arrow), Resolution 106, the Gaza protests, the fedayeen, and the dispute over consequences

sources.label: Letter from the representative of Egypt to the President of the Security Council, 1 March 1955 (S/3365), UNISPAL
"Operation Black Arrow", IDF and Defense Establishment Archives, Israel Ministry of Defense
Security Council Resolution 106 (1955) of 29 March 1955, UNISPAL
"The March 1955 Outburst in the Gaza Strip", PalQuest, Institute for Palestine Studies
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", IJMES 36:4 (2004)
Memorandum of conversation, Eban, Rafael, Salmon, Allen and Bergus, 11 October 1955 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 333)
Solod–Nasser conversation, 15 June 1954 (AVPRF; trans. Guy Laron), Wilson Center Digital Archive

claims.text: Israel's Defense Ministry archive dates Operation Black Arrow to 28 February 1955, says it followed a series of border incidents ending with an Egyptian intelligence squad's infiltration and the murder of an Israeli citizen, and records thirty-eight Egyptian soldiers and eight Israelis killed.

Egypt's letter to the Security Council of 1 March 1955 described a force of about two platoons that advanced some 3 km, blew up an army camp and a water-pump house, and ambushed a relief platoon of 35; it gave 37 members of the armed forces and 2 civilians killed and 30 soldiers and 2 civilians injured.

On 6 March 1955 the Egyptian–Israeli Mixed Armistice Commission found that a "planned attack ordered by Israel authorities" had been "committed by Israel regular army forces against the Egyptian regular army force"; Resolution 106 of 29 March 1955, adopted unanimously at the 695th meeting, condemned it as a violation of the cease-fire and "inconsistent with the obligations of the parties".
Shlaim gives 38 Egyptian soldiers killed and 31 wounded and writes that the raid "seriously destabilised" Nasser's regime.

On 1 March 1955 a mass demonstration in Gaza chanted against relocation and "US agents"; Egyptian police fired and killed a textile worker, Hosni Belal. Protesters demanded cancellation of the Sinai resettlement plan (12,000 refugee families, agreed by Egypt in 1953), arms and training for camp residents, and civil freedoms.

The protests were organized jointly by communists and the Muslim Brotherhood through a Supreme National Committee (Mu'in Bseiso of the Palestinian Communist Party and Fathi al-Balaawi of the Brotherhood negotiated with Egyptian officials); Gaza's military governor promised to end the relocation scheme, then ordered mass arrests on the night of 8–9 March 1955 and held detainees until July 1957.
In September 1955 Egypt formed Palestinian fida'i units (Battalion 141) under Lt. Col. Mustafa Hafez, based in Gaza; their operations ran until Israeli intelligence assassinated Hafez in July 1956.
Shlaim's reading: Nasser sought arms after the raid, ending in the Czech deal, and "by pressing its military advantage too far, Israel inadvertently helped to push Egypt into the arms of Moscow".

On 11 October 1955 Assistant Secretary George Allen and Ambassador Eban both treated the Gaza raid as a turning point but disagreed on its cause: Allen said Nasser was "deeply impressed" by reports of Israeli superiority; Eban argued that the Turkish–Iraqi pact, not the raid, changed Nasser's attitude.
A Soviet record shows Nasser formally asking about Soviet arms on 15 June 1954, eight months before the raid.

disputes.question: Did the Gaza raid push Egypt to the Soviet bloc for arms?

positions.view: Yes, decisively: the raid destabilised the regime and drove the search for arms that ended in the Czech deal (Shlaim; Allen in October 1955).
Not by itself: the Baghdad Pact changed Nasser's course (Eban), and Nasser had already asked Moscow about arms in June 1954 (Soviet record).

disputes.question: How many were killed in the Gaza raid?

positions.view: 38 Egyptian soldiers and 8 Israelis (Israel's Defense Ministry archive); 38 killed and 31 wounded (Shlaim).
37 soldiers and 2 civilians killed, 32 injured (Egypt's letter to the Council); 38 dead and 33 injured (PalQuest).

entries.topic: The Baghdad Pact (1955), Bandung (April 1955), and Jordan's crisis to Glubb's dismissal (December 1955–March 1956)

sources.label: Pact of Mutual Cooperation between Iraq and Turkey (the Baghdad Pact), 24 February 1955, Avalon Project
Memorandum from Rountree to the Acting Secretary of State with position paper on the Baghdad Pact, November 1956 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XII, doc. 145)
"Bandung Conference", Encyclopedia.com (entries from Zachary Karabell, Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa, and the Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict)
"Arabs Seek Censure of Israel at Bandung Asian-African Conference", Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 15 April 1955
"Palestine at Bandung: How the historic Asian-African conference challenged imperialism", Middle East Eye (2024)
"Hussein's Early Reign", Jordan: A Country Study, Library of Congress Federal Research Division
Report from Amman on the dismissal of Glubb Pasha, 11 March 1956, Wilson Center Digital Archive

claims.text: Iraq and Turkey signed the Pact of Mutual Cooperation at Baghdad on 24 February 1955; Article 1 bound them to "co-operate for their security and defence"; Article 5 opened accession to "any member of the Arab League" or other state concerned with regional security and recognized by both; it ran five years, renewable.
Britain adhered on 5 April 1955, Pakistan on 23 September 1955 and Iran on 23 October 1955 (dates as given in the Avalon footnote).

The United States never signed; a November 1956 State Department position paper said joining "would not serve the U.S. national interest" because it would revive Israeli demands for a US security guarantee and complicate Senate ratification, entangle Washington in Hashemite–Saudi–Egyptian rivalries, and provoke the USSR.

Washington nonetheless joined the Pact's Economic and Counter-Subversion Committees in April 1956, set up a military liaison group in Baghdad on 1 November 1956, and paid a one-sixth share ($76,350) of the $459,746 administrative budget.

The Asian-African Conference met at Bandung on 18–24 April 1955 with twenty-nine states, convened by the prime ministers of Pakistan, India, Burma, Ceylon and Indonesia; Karabell writes that it "saw Nasser emerge as an international leader".
Israel was not invited, despite the insistence of Burma's U Nu (JTA); Middle East Eye adds that Nehru and U Nu tried to have Israel invited and Indonesia "vehemently opposed" it.

Before the conference Arab delegations sought a resolution condemning Israel; Nehru was reported cool to it and India's delegate Arthur Lall said it "remains to be seen" whether it would reach the floor.

The final communiqué declared "support for the rights of the Arab people of Palestine" and called for implementation of the UN resolutions on Palestine and a peaceful settlement; Haj Amin al-Husseini attended as part of Yemen's delegation.

In December 1955, after a British military delegation visited Amman, Prime Minister Hazza al-Majali said he would take Jordan into the Baghdad Pact; three days of rioting followed, the Arab Legion restored order and his government resigned within a week.
In March 1956 King Hussein dismissed Glubb as commander of the Arab Legion; the force was renamed the Jordan Arab Army, British officers were phased out, and Ali Abu Nuwar succeeded him.

A report from Amman dated 11 March 1956 says Glubb was given about 19 hours and left on 2 March, and lists among the triggers his "open endorsement of Hazza' al-Majali and the supporters of the Baghdad Pact" and a radio station that attacked Egypt while defending Iraq.
In Jordan's elections of 21 October 1956 the National Socialist Party won a plurality and Hussein named its leader, Sulayman Nabulsi, an admirer of Nasser, prime minister.

entries.topic: Operation Alpha, Dulles's address of 26 August 1955, and the Anderson mission (December 1954–March 1956)

sources.label: "Operation Alpha", Jewish Virtual Library
"Operation Alpha (1955)", ECF Interactive Database (Economic Cooperation Foundation)
John Foster Dulles, "American Policy Toward the Middle East", address to the Council on Foreign Relations, New York, 26 August 1955 (text), Jewish Virtual Library
Telegram 421 from the Department of State to the Embassy in Egypt, 1 September 1955 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 248)
FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XV, chapter "Continued U.S. Consideration of Funding the Aswan High Dam and the Anderson Mission" (documents 121–150, February–March 1956)
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", IJMES 36:4 (2004)

claims.text: 'Alpha' was the State Department's code word for a secret US–British effort to devise an Arab–Israeli settlement; on 20 December 1954 Dulles assigned Francis Russell to coordinate with his British counterpart, Evelyn Shuckburgh.

The terms the two governments reached in 1955 included Israeli cession of parts of the Negev to Egypt and Jordan to create a land link between them, resettlement of 75,000 Palestinian refugees in Israel, and non-belligerence "in lieu of peace".

In his address of 26 August 1955 Dulles named three problems: "the tragic plight of the 900,000 refugees", "the pall of fear that hangs over the Arab and Israel people alike", and the lack of fixed permanent boundaries.

He proposed that refugees live in dignity "through resettlement and, to such an extent as may be feasible, repatriation", said "Compensation is due from Israel to the refugees", and suggested an international loan to which Eisenhower would recommend "substantial participation by the United States".

Dulles said Eisenhower would recommend formal US treaty engagements "to prevent or thwart any effort by either side to alter by force" agreed boundaries, called the armistice lines not "permanent frontiers in every respect", and backed UN review of Jerusalem and shared use of the Jordan Valley rivers.

On 1 September 1955 the Department told its Cairo embassy to reassure Nasser that the speech did not exclude some refugees returning to Israel, that the guarantee treaties concerned only Arab–Israeli borders, not Middle East defence, and that the proposals were "only a beginning"; Egypt's Fawzi was reported saying there was "no plan" to discuss the speech seriously.

Facing Egyptian and Israeli opposition, Eisenhower sent Robert Anderson, a Texas lawyer and personal friend, on a secret CIA-supported mission between January and March 1956 to Ben-Gurion, Sharett and Nasser; both sides rejected the plan.
On 27 February 1956 Eisenhower approved letters to Ben-Gurion and Nasser for Anderson to carry on his return trip ("The President went over these drafts and approved them").

Shlaim records that after the Gaza raid Israeli diplomats shifted from seeking a defence pact to seeking arms, and that in April 1956 the United States gave its final rejection of Israel's arms request.

entries.topic: The Egyptian–Czechoslovak arms deal (September 1955), Israel's arms requests to Washington, and the turn to French Mystères (1955–1956)

sources.label: "The Egyptian Czech Arms Deal", Jewish Virtual Library
Telegram 632 from the Embassy in Egypt (Allen and Byroade on their meeting with Nasser), c. 1 October 1955 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 321)
Memorandum of conversation, Hoover, Murphy, Allen with Eban, Shiloah and Salmon, 16 November 1955 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 413)
Telegram from the Embassy in Israel, received 3 January 1956 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XV, doc. 2)
Memorandum from Rountree to Hoover on possible additional French Mystère deliveries to Israel, 20 September 1956 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XVI, doc. 242)
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", IJMES 36:4 (2004)
"Don't Give a Dam: The Feud over Financing the Aswan High Dam", Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (oral histories)
Memorandum of conversation, Eban, Rafael, Salmon, Allen and Bergus, 11 October 1955 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 333)

claims.text: Nasser announced on 27 September 1955 that Czechoslovakia would supply Soviet heavy weapons to Egypt — tanks, MiG-15 fighters and bombers — in a deal the Jewish Virtual Library values at "more than $83 million"; Nasser called it "unconditional".

Meeting Allen and Byroade around 1 October 1955, Nasser said Egypt had already sent one million Egyptian pounds to Prague "on account", that cotton and rice would be shipped "more or less parallel" with the arms, and that the agreement was "without any conditions whatsoever"; Byroade had reported on 29 September that the "actual agreement on arms was with Czechoslovakia".

Assistant Secretary Allen told Eban on 11 October 1955 that the deal "would go through", would not be "of token proportions", and that Nasser had first presented it as trading "cotton which Egypt could not sell elsewhere for arms which Egypt could not obtain elsewhere"; he added that the sticking point in US arms talks had been the US requirement for a military mission, not a non-aggression pledge.

On 16 November 1955 Eban presented a confidential list of arms "solely for defensive purposes", saying the request "sprang directly" from the imbalance created by the Czech deal and that Israel had not obtained any Mystères from France despite press reports; Hoover said the US had to consider the other Tripartite signatories.

In late December 1955 Sharett stressed Israel's "almost complete lack of defensive facilities" against Egyptian jets; Israel wanted twelve Mystère IVs ordered from France, whose release the French said rested "entirely with US Government"; the first 15 MiGs had reached Egypt about two months earlier.

Shlaim writes that Dulles had decided on the eve of the Kinneret raid to sell Israel defensive arms, that Eban was told on 13 December 1955 the decision was postponed, and that the final US refusal came in April 1956; Sharett wrote: "My world became black, the matter of arms was murdered."

Shlaim presents the French orientation as the result of American refusal: Peres went directly to the French defence establishment, and "France offered arms in the hope of inducing Israel to go to war against Egypt" while "America allowed its allies to supply arms to Israel on condition that Israel did not go to war."

A State Department memorandum of 20 September 1956 said Israel, believed to have 24 Mystères, "appears possible" to have 48; British sources reported "forty-eight Mystere IVs from France", eighteen aircraft seen passing through Brindisi may have been heading to Israel, and France had proposed selling 24 more through the Near East Arms Coordinating Committee, which Washington called undesirable.

entries.topic: The Kinneret raid and Resolution 111, Hammarskjöld's cease-fire mission, and the border to October 1956

sources.label: Security Council Resolution 111 (1956) of 19 January 1956, UNISPAL
Editorial note on the Lake Tiberias incident and the Security Council (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XIV, doc. 453)
Yearbook of the United Nations 1956, Part I, Section 1, Chapter 1 (the Palestine question)
Avi Shlaim, "Israel between East and West, 1948–1956", IJMES 36:4 (2004)
Telegram from the Embassy in Israel, received 3 January 1956 (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XV, doc. 2)

claims.text: On the night of 11–12 December 1955 Israeli regular forces attacked Syrian army positions east of Lake Tiberias; Syria complained to the Council on 13 December.

Shlaim writes that the operation (Olive Leaves) was authorized by Ben-Gurion alone while Sharett was in Washington seeking arms, quoting Sharett's jibe that "Ben-Gurion the defence minister consulted with Ben-Gurion the foreign minister" and Eban's comment that "the short-term objective had triumphed unduly over our long-term aims".

UNTSO's Chief of Staff reported on 15 and 30 December 1955 that Israel linked the attack to Syrian fire on Israeli fishing boats and police escorts, and found a "striking disparity between the scale of retaliation and the provocation".
The US Embassy reported that Sharett, without condemning the government's action, appeared to regard it "as a severe blunder".

Resolution 111 of 19 January 1956, adopted unanimously at the 715th meeting on a US–British–French draft, condemned the attack as "a flagrant violation" of the cease-fire, the Israel–Syria Armistice Agreement and the Charter, held that Syrian interference on the lake "in no way justifies the Israel action", and warned that the Council would otherwise "have to consider what further measures under the Charter are required".

On 4 April 1956 the Council unanimously asked the Secretary-General to survey compliance; he visited the region from 10 April to 3 May 1956 and reported on 9 May that the governments had given cease-fire assurances, observing it "unconditionally" if the other side complied, while reserving self-defence under Article 51.

On 4 June 1956 the Council unanimously endorsed his view that full compliance with the armistice "represents a stage which has to be passed" before progress on the main issues, and declared that UN observers' freedom of movement "must be respected".

In mid-August 1956 mines and attacks near the Gaza Strip killed four Israeli citizens and wounded eight; the next day an Egyptian car carrying medical personnel was ambushed in Egyptian-controlled territory and nine Egyptians were killed.

On the night of 10–11 October 1956 Israeli forces demolished the police post at Qalqilya in Jordan with explosives, inflicting "heavy casualties" (the Yearbook gives no figure); other incidents that summer included Sheikh Abd el Aziz and Mount Scopus (24–25 July) and Sharafi near Husan (25–26 September).

entries.topic: The Aswan High Dam offer and its withdrawal (December 1955–19 July 1956) and the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company (26 July 1956)

sources.label: Memorandum of conversation, Eisenhower, Dulles and Hoover, White House, 19 July 1956, 9:40–9:52 a.m. (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XV, doc. 473)
Memorandum of conversation, Dulles and Ambassador Ahmed Hussein, Department of State, 19 July 1956, 4:10–5:07 p.m. (FRUS 1955–1957, vol. XV, doc. 478)
"Don't Give a Dam: The Feud over Financing the Aswan High Dam", Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training (oral histories of Parker Hart, Robert Bowie, James Cortada, Fraser Wilkins)
"The Suez Crisis, 1956", Milestones in the History of U.S. Foreign Relations, Office of the Historian

claims.text: The joint US–UK–World Bank offer to finance the High Dam dated from 16 December 1955; by July 1956 Egypt's ambassador was returning to Washington to announce acceptance.

Parker Hart recalled that the US was prepared to grant about $56 million at once, with roughly 85% of the grant share from the US and 15% from Britain, and that the US loan was conditioned on Egyptian fiscal reforms and a prior Egypt–Sudan Nile agreement; Nasser objected: "This is a denigration of Egypt."

On the morning of 19 July 1956 Eisenhower agreed with Dulles that "we should withdraw the U.S. offer upon the occasion of the Ambassador's visit", citing Egypt's changed economic conditions, the unresolved Nile waters dispute, the unpopularity that austerity would bring to whoever built the dam, and growing difficulty in working with Nasser's government.

That afternoon Dulles told Ambassador Ahmed Hussein it was "not feasible at present" to proceed, put the cost at $1.3 billion including $900 million internal, said "no single project in the Mutual Security Program was as unpopular today", and that the dam should be "put on the shelf"; he added that basic opposition came from a feeling that Egypt was working with those "hostile to us".

Hussein replied that the dam was "the only solution to the population problem", that Moscow was making a "very generous" offer, and that "there were strong pressures which Nasser might not be able to resist"; Dulles said a Soviet offer would be made "for political purposes".

In the oral histories, Robert Bowie said Congress was turning hostile — cotton growers, Israel's supporters and the China lobby — and threatened legislation forbidding aid funds for the dam; Fraser Wilkins called Congress the "real reason"; Parker Hart called Dulles's decision "impulsive"; and the ADST compilation itself says the Czech arms deal and Egypt's recognition of Communist China angered Dulles.

On 26 July 1956 Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company, offering full compensation; the Office of the Historian notes the company had been jointly British-French owned and operated.
Bowie recalled the nationalization came "within a matter of ten days" of the withdrawal; Egypt then turned to the Soviet Union, which Wilkins said made it a "$600 million project under the Russians".

disputes.question: Why did Washington withdraw the Aswan offer?

positions.view: Policy judgement on Egypt itself: changed economics, the Nile dispute, austerity, Nasser's ties with the Soviet bloc (the 19 July memoranda).
Domestic politics: congressional hostility from cotton growers, supporters of Israel and the China lobby made funding impossible (Bowie, Wilkins).
Dulles's own impulsive decision (Hart) or a trap set by Nasser (Cortada).

entries.topic: "Under God" (February–June 1954) and "In God We Trust" (1955–1956): the American home front in its documented anti-communist frame

sources.label: Brian Kaylor, "One Nation Divisible?", Liberty magazine
Isaac Kramnick, "'Under God' marries religion to citizenship", convention speech, Freedom From Religion Foundation
"Statement by the President Upon Signing Bill To Include the Words 'Under God' in the Pledge to the Flag", 14 June 1954, American Presidency Project
House Report 112-47 (2011), reaffirming "In God We Trust" as the national motto, govinfo
S. Con. Res. 96 (109th Congress), on the 50th anniversary of the national motto, govinfo
"President Eisenhower signs 'In God We Trust' into law", HISTORY.com, This Day in History, 30 July

claims.text: On 7 February 1954 the Rev. George Docherty preached at New York Avenue Presbyterian Church in Washington, with Eisenhower in attendance, that "there was something missing in this Pledge" and that "an atheistic American is a contradiction in terms".
Kramnick quotes the sermon's Cold War framing: Docherty said he "could hear little Muscovites repeat a similar pledge to their hammer and sickle flag" and that "it is a theological war".
Members of Congress introduced bills after the sermon and the change passed both houses in under four months; Eisenhower signed it on Flag Day, 14 June 1954.

Eisenhower's signing statement said "the millions of our school children will daily proclaim" the nation's dedication to God, that "we are reaffirming the transcendence of religious faith in America's heritage and future", and spoke of "those spiritual weapons which forever will be our country's most powerful resource".
In 1955 Congress made "In God We Trust" a mandatory inscription on all US currency and coins; it first appeared on paper money in 1957, on the one-dollar silver certificate.
On 30 July 1956 Eisenhower signed H.J. Res. 396 (84th Congress), Public Law 84-851 (Act of July 30, 1956, ch. 795; 70 Stat. 732), now 36 U.S.C. §302: "'In God we trust' is the national motto."
The House Judiciary Committee's report on H.J. Res. 396, dated 28 March 1956, said it would be "of great spiritual and psychological value to our country to have a clearly designated national motto".

HISTORY.com attributes the 1956 motto law to Public Law 84-140 and says it also put the motto on paper money; the House report gives P.L. 84-851 for the motto, and the Senate resolution dates the currency requirement to 1955.

None of these sources documents any link between the 1954 and 1956 changes and Israel or Zionist organizations; the documented framing is religious revival and anti-communism. Any reading that connects them to Israel would be interpretation without a documentary basis in these sources.

disputes.question: Which public law made 'In God We Trust' the national motto?

positions.view: P.L. 84-851, 30 July 1956, 70 Stat. 732 (House Report 112-47).
P.L. 84-140 (HISTORY.com), which other sources treat as the 1955 currency law.

entries.topic: Angleton's Counterintelligence Staff and the Israel account (1954) and the Khrushchev speech (1956)

sources.label: David Robarge (CIA Chief Historian), "Cunning Passages, Contrived Corridors: Wandering in the Angletonian Wilderness", Studies in Intelligence, Center for the Study of Intelligence
Shammai Siskind, "Israel and the Great Powers: The Unsung Cold War Role", Middle East Quarterly 27:2 (Spring 2020)
"Viktor Graevsky, who passed Khrushchev's report to the Mossad, has died" (in Russian), NEWSru.co.il, 21 October 2007

claims.text: The CIA's historian writes that James Angleton became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954, and that his "control of that country's account at CIA, an administrative anomaly, was one of the foundations of his influence".
Robarge writes that Angleton "ardently supported Israel" and "saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union".

Khrushchev delivered his 'secret speech' to a closed session of the Twentieth Party Congress in February 1956; Victor Grayevsky, a Polish Jewish journalist, borrowed a copy from the Polish Communist Party office where his girlfriend worked and gave it to Yaakov Barmor, a Shin Bet agent, who photographed it.

Siskind writes that Ben-Gurion sent a copy to Washington by courier to Israel's liaison Izzy Dorot, that on the US side only Angleton was to see it, that it reached Allen Dulles by mid-April 1956, and that the CIA gave the text to The New York Times in early June 1956.

NEWSru.co.il, reporting Grayevsky's death in October 2007, says he immigrated to Israel in 1957, served for fourteen years as a double agent reporting KGB contacts to the Shin Bet until 1971, and was honoured by Shin Bet chief Avi Dichter in August 2006; it names both the Mossad and the Shin Bet as recipients of the speech, without resolving which.

Neither the CIA historian nor these accounts documents a formal written liaison agreement in 1954–1956; Siskind says only that the US had agreed "a few years earlier" to cooperate with Israel on intelligence.

entries.topic: After the coup: the Iranian oil consortium (October 1953–October 1954)

sources.label: Editorial note on Herbert Hoover Jr.'s appointment and the consortium proposal (FRUS 1951–1954, Iran, doc. 331)
Telegram from Dulles to the Embassy in Iran conveying Hoover's message on ratification, October 1954 (FRUS 1952–1954, vol. X, doc. 502)
British Foreign Office statement on the Iranian oil consortium, 5 August 1954 (reproduced by the Mossadegh Project)
Joint statement of the Iranian and United Kingdom delegations on compensation to the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, Tehran, 5 August 1954 (reproduced by the Mossadegh Project)
Department of State press release, "Arrangements for Participation in Iranian Oil Consortium", 7 December 1954, Department of State Bulletin XXXI:809 (reproduced by the Mossadegh Project)

claims.text: Herbert Hoover Jr. was appointed on 14 October 1953 as the Secretary of State's consultant on the Anglo-Iranian oil dispute and visited Iran from 17 October to 4 November 1953.

On 1 November 1953 Foreign Minister Entezam proposed an international consortium buying oil from the National Iranian Oil Company, in which the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company could take part without majority control; a British–Iranian communiqué of 5 December 1953 promised a solution taking account of "the national aspirations of the Persian people" regarding their resources.

The agreement in principle with the consortium was signed on 5 August 1954; the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company took a 40% holding and Royal Dutch Shell 14%, the rest going to American and French companies, with two operating companies incorporated in the Netherlands.

Five American companies — Gulf, Socony-Vacuum, Standard Oil (New Jersey), Standard Oil of California and the Texas Company — each held 8%, and could transfer up to one-eighth of their share to other American firms within six months.
Iran agreed to pay the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company a net £25 million in compensation over ten years, interest-free, beginning 1 January 1957.

Iran's Senate passed the oil bill on 28 October 1954 by 41 to 4 with 3 abstentions, the Shah signed it on 29 October, and the agreements took effect that day; Hoover called it a "significant victory".
By arithmetic from these figures (40% + 14% + 5 × 8%), 6% remained for the French participant; the Foreign Office statement itself says only "American and French companies".
